title: Ser or estar
subtitle: Two Spanish verbs for “is”, and the two questions that pick one

scenes.narration: In English, "is" is just "is". In Spanish you have to choose between two verbs, and learners pick the wrong one all the time.
scenes.question: ¿Es o está?

sides.label: estar
sides.note: where it is, and how it is **right now**

steps.say: Es comes from the verb ser. It says what something is, and what it is like.
Está comes from estar. It says where something is, and how it is right now.

scenes.title: The same subject, both verbs
scenes.narration: Listen to the same subject with each verb.

rows.label: The soup
cells: La sopa [**es**]{accent} de tomate. · It is tomato soup.
La sopa [**está**]{warn} fría. · The soup is cold.

rows.label: Madrid
cells: Madrid [**está**]{warn} en España. · Madrid is in Spain.

rows.label: Today
cells: Hoy [**está**]{warn} nublado. · It is cloudy today.

steps.say: Ana es alta. Ana is tall. That is what she is like. Ana está cansada. Ana is tired. That is how she is right now.
The soup is tomato soup. That is what it is. But it is cold right now, so, está.
Madrid is huge, with es. But where Madrid is, in Spain, takes está. Even though it is never going to move.
Today is Monday takes es: days and times are what something is. But the weather right now takes está.

scenes.title: Which verb?
scenes.narration: So here is the whole decision, as two questions.

steps.say: Ana is tall. It does not say where, and it is not a passing state. So, es.
Ana is tired. That is how she is right now. Está.
Madrid is in Spain. It says where, and Madrid is a place, not an event. Está.
But this last branch is the one that trips everybody up.

scenes.title: Where a party is
scenes.narration: Here is the trap. Both of these sentences say where something is.
scenes.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 1600 760"><g id="party"><text id="s1" x="800" y="140" font-size="60" text-anchor="middle">La fiesta <tspan id="s1-verb" class="fill-accent">es</tspan> <tspan id="s1-after">en mi casa.</tspan></text><text id="s1-en" x="800" y="208" font-size="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">The party is at my house.</text></g><g id="keys"><text id="s2" x="800" y="330" font-size="60" text-anchor="middle">Las llaves <tspan id="s2-verb" class="fill-warn">están</tspan> <tspan id="s2-after">en mi casa.</tspan></text><text id="s2-en" x="800" y="398" font-size="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">The keys are at my house.</text></g><g id="talk"><text id="s3" x="800" y="560" font-size="60" text-anchor="middle">La conferencia <tspan id="s3-verb" class="fill-accent">es</tspan> <tspan id="s3-after">en el Aula Magna.</tspan></text><text id="s3-en" x="800" y="628" font-size="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">The talk is in the main hall.</text><text id="source" x="800" y="690" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--faint)">Example from the Real Academia Española, Nueva gramática §37.8f</text></g></svg>

steps.say: The keys are at my house. Keys are things, and where a thing is takes estar. Están.
The party is at my house. A party is not a thing sitting somewhere. It is an event, so where it happens takes ser. Es.
The Royal Spanish Academy gives this example. The talk is in the main hall. It means the talk takes place there, so it is es.
So if you could swap in "takes place", use es.

scenes.title: One adjective, two meanings
scenes.narration: And sometimes the verb changes what the word means.

steps.say: Es aburrido means he is boring. Está aburrido means he is bored. Not the same thing at all.
Es listo, he is clever. Está listo, he is ready.
And es rico is rich. But say the food está rica, and you mean it is tasty.

scenes.narration: So, four things to keep in your head.
scenes.headline: Ask two questions
items: [**es**]{accent}: what it is, what it is like, days and times
[**está**]{warn}: where a thing or a person is

steps.say: Es for what something is, what it is like, and days and times.
Es for where an event happens.
Está for where a thing or a person is.
And está for how it is right now. That covers almost every sentence you will meet.
